generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, judging a source means weighing it against explicit criteria rather than trusting a first impression. Source type comes first, since a peer-reviewed study, a review, an official report and a popular article carry very different weight. Currency depends on the question you are asking, authority rests on who stands behind the work and how it has been checked, and relevance asks whether the source actually speaks to your question, not merely to its topic.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who each find a source for the same essay and must decide whether to use it.

{{learner-a}} finds a recent, well-written article that states the claim clearly, and uses it straight away. It is current and readable, so it seems ideal. But {{learner-a}} has not asked what type of source it is or who stands behind it. It turns out to be a popular piece summarising someone else's work, with no review and no named expertise. The appraisal stopped at how the source read.

{{learner-b}} finds the same article and runs it through the criteria. It is current and on topic, but its type is journalism rather than research, and its authority is thin for the claim being made. {{learner-b}} traces it back to the original study it summarises, checks how that study was done, and uses that instead, noting the article is useful only for framing. The weaker source is set aside, with a reason.

Both students found a usable-looking source. Only {{learner-b}} judged it against explicit criteria, and could justify the choice.
generatedProse.summary: Evaluating a source well means weighing it against explicit criteria rather than a first impression. Source type sets what the evidence can support, currency is judged against your question, authority rests on who produced the work and how it was checked, and relevance asks what the source actually examines. You can now appraise a source against these criteria, judge how its type bears on its use, and justify what you keep and set aside. The next lesson widens the net past a single starting search.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s appraisal rigorous rather than impressionistic?

items.text: Weighing the source's type and authority, not just how recent and readable it was, and tracing it back to the original study.
Reading the article more slowly and carefully than the other student did.
Preferring the article because it was clearly written.
Choosing the most recent source available.

feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing type and authority, and going back to the study behind the article, is a rigorous appraisal.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} weighed beyond how the article read.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}}'s appraisal was rigorous because it weighed source type and authority, not just recency and readability, and traced the claim back to the original study.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
